title: NorthForge — tokenstream characterization and hosting decision
summary: Discovery focused on p95 streaming latency targets, steady-state token/sec, and deciding between Hosted, Dedicated and Private deployment. Customer emphasized strict p95 <= 200ms for short responses, required encryption/KMS controls, and a pilot to benchmark token/sec with their prompt mix.
action_items: Maya Chen: Share tailored benchmark plan and sample harness (due: 2029-12-14)
Diego Ramos: Provide recommended batching and cache config for their median seqlen (due: 2029-12-16)
Priya Singh: Send list of compliance docs they need (due: 2029-12-13)
next_steps: Run 48-hour pilot on Redwood Hosted using customer prompt set (AE to set up trial access)
SE to provide a perf harness and starter k6 script, include KV cache toggles
Schedule deep dive with SecOps on Private deployment checklist (tentative 2029-12-18)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-12-11
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54 min
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Arjun Patel (Redwood Solutions); Lena Park (Head of ML - NorthForge), Tomás Rivera (Platform), Priya Singh (SecOps), Evan Cole (SRE), Jordan Li (PM)

Summary: quick intro, target p95 numbers, current infra (on-prem + GCP), tokens/sec targets, streaming behavior and tail latencies, security/Governance constraints, decision criteria and next steps.

00:00 - Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time, hi Lena, Tomás, Priya, Evan, Jordan. Quick roundtable and then Diego will jump into the perf questions.
00:12 - Lena Park: Hi Maya, thanks. I'll hand it over to Tomás for infra details but our primary ask is: we need p95s under 200 milliseconds for short, user-facing replies and we want to understand the Hosted versus Dedicated tradeoffs.
00:26 - Tomás Rivera: Yeah, for context we have a mix — some inference runs in GCP, some older services on-prem. We've been prototyping with the open models but can't match the latency consistently under load.
00:39 - Diego Ramos: Totally, thanks. Couple clarifying q's up front: what's your typical sequence length distribution and what's your mix of streaming vs full-response? Are you doing few-shot prompts?
00:54 - Jordan Li: Most of our user flows are short: median prompt ~25 tokens, median completion ~40 tokens. But we have a secondary analytical route that's 1k–2k tokens. Streaming is used only for the short conversational flows.
01:10 - Maya Chen: So p95 is driven by the short flows — that's where customer experience matters. Diego, feel free to ask about concurrency profile.
01:19 - Diego Ramos: Right. How many concurrent users (or concurrent streams) do you plan to support at p95 SLA?
01:28 - Lena Park: Initial target is 300 concurrent conversational users in region during peaks, with headroom to 1k in Q2 next year.
01:37 - Evan Cole: Also important: we cannot accept any secrets leaving our VPC for production — so Private deployment is on the table, but we'd like to see Hosted economics first.
01:49 - Priya Singh: And from SecOps side, SOC 2 and customer-managed KMS are must-haves. We need audit logs for token-level request tracing, or at least request-level traces tied to SSO identities.
02:03 - Diego Ramos: Understood. For the p95 ~200ms target on short streams, there are a few levers: 1) model choice and smaller context sizes, 2) continuous batching strategy, 3) prefix/K-V caching for repeated prompts, and 4) routing to dedicated capacity to avoid noisy neighbors.
02:21 - Tomás Rivera: When you say K-V caching, do you mean the attention KV cache stored between requests or a higher-level prefix cache?
02:29 - Diego Ramos: Both patterns exist. We support prefix caching (re-usable prompt prefixes) and efficient KV cache reuse in the runtime to avoid re-computing early layers. For short responses, prefix caching often yields biggest wins.
02:41 - Jordan Li: Any rule-of-thumb for tokens/sec per GPU for our median seqlen?
02:47 - Diego Ramos: Ballpark for an optimized FP16-ish run: for median 70 tokens per request, a single A100-style GPU can do ~1,200–1,800 tokens/sec depending on model and quantization. With quantized int8 kernels that we recommend for Dedicated, you can push that higher but watch quality shifts.
03:03 - Lena Park: So to hit 300 concurrent users with streaming p95 200ms, what's our expected fleet size?
03:10 - Diego Ramos: If you want headroom for concurrency and multiplexing, you usually plan around throughput rather than pure concurrency. Example: if each active user streams at avg 5 tokens/sec during a session, 300 users is ~1.5k tokens/sec sustained. That maps to about 1 GPU in the optimistic case for smaller models, but with p95 SLOs and spikes I'd recommend a 2–3 GPU Dedicated pool or Hosted reserved capacity with burst.
03:31 - Tomás Rivera: That seems small — are you assuming tiny models? We're evaluating mid-size open models, not nano models.
03:38 - Diego Ramos: Right — that estimate depends a lot on model family. For mid-size 7B-ish models, throughput per GPU drops — maybe 400–800 tokens/sec, so you'd need 2–4 GPUs. For MPT-style bigger or 13B, that's another multiplier. We'll send model-specific numbers in the calc.
03:55 - Maya Chen: We should also talk about tail latencies. p95 at 200ms doesn't capture occasional cold starts or cache misses. Diego, can you explain how Redwood handles cold-token tail?
04:05 - Diego Ramos: Sure. The runtime uses warm pools and continuous batching. For streaming, we maintain pinned KV contexts where appropriate. Cold starts mainly happen when the model isn't loaded or after eviction. For Hosted we have warm pools in each region; Dedicated gives you pinned GPUs so cold starts are essentially eliminated. Private can be configured the same way but it's on your infra ops.
04:26 - Priya Singh: For Private, how do updates and kernel changes get pushed? We can't have arbitrary remote code execution into our cluster.
04:33 - Arjun Patel: For Private, we ship a customer-controlled control plane that pulls signed releases. For critical environments we offer an on-prem bundle that your infra team applies, and we integrate with your PKI so only signed artifacts are accepted.
04:44 - Priya Singh: Good, need to see that in writing.
04:47 - Jordan Li: Back on perf — what's the expected impact of enabling quantization vs leaving FP16 for quality? We have an NPS-like metric tied to hallucination rates.
04:56 - Diego Ramos: Quantization to int8 can reduce latency and increase tokens/sec by 1.5–2x in many cases, but model-specific quality drops are model-and-prompt dependent. We recommend running a small quality regression set as part of the pilot. Redwood Optimize will give suggested quant profiles per workload.
05:12 - Tomás Rivera: Can you run streaming benchmarks with and without prefix cache so we can see realistic p95 tails?
05:19 - Maya Chen: Yes — that's exactly what we'll include in the benchmark plan. We'll toggle prefix cache on/off and compare p50/p95/p99.
05:26 - Lena Park: Also need to test routing fallbacks — if Dedicated pool saturates, how does Redwood fallback to Hosted without leaking data between tenants?
05:35 - Diego Ramos: Fallbacks follow policy: you can restrict fallback to model variants that don't use your customer data, or route only to compatible Dedicated regions. Hosted fallback for production typically only used if the customer allows encrypted payload forwarding; otherwise we'd fail open or use a lower-tier Dedicated queue. We'll add recommended fallback rules for your security posture.
05:55 - Evan Cole: Any synchronous APIs vs streaming differences for latency measurement? Our client library prefers streaming to reduce perceived latency.
06:03 - Diego Ramos: Streaming reduces perceived latency but requires more careful multiplexing — the runtime manages partial token emit and backpressure. For measuring p95 perceived latency, measure time to first token and p95 of that. For NorthForge short flows, first-token p95 is the critical SLI.
06:20 - Jordan Li: What about multiplexing for many small flows — do you batch across requests or rely on continuous batching per GPU?
06:28 - Diego Ramos: Continuous batching is the core; we also use opportunistic multiplexing across in-flight streams. That introduces a scheduling decision — lower latency SLOs mean stricter batch cutoffs which reduce throughput. We'll show the latency vs cost curve in the deck.
06:44 - Maya Chen: Quick question, Lena — what's your timeline to choose a hosting path?
06:49 - Lena Park: We hope to decide by end of Q1; pilot in Jan, production by Q3. Security sign-off is long lead — probably takes 6–8 weeks after pilot.
06:59 - Priya Singh: We'll need SOC 2 Type II and a dedicated audit window. Also need to understand data retention policies on Hosted.
07:08 - Diego Ramos: On Hosted, by default we retain request metadata for 30 days for observability; for enterprise customers we can extend retention or configure zero-log modes. For Private, logs live in your cluster and retention is yours.
07:22 - Tomás Rivera: Can Redwood instrument request-level token counts and send that as metrics? We need billing alignment and cost visibility.
07:29 - Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood Console exposes token-level breakdowns and per-route cost. We'll include sample screenshots in the follow-up.
07:36 - Jordan Li: For the pilot we'll need a k6 script or similar to emulate our session patterns. Does Redwood have a starter harness?
07:42 - Diego Ramos: We do. We'll share a starter harness that can run streaming workloads, toggle caching, and synthesize your token distribution. We'll also provide a lightweight client that emits streaming frames so you measure first-token times correctly.
07:58 - Evan Cole: Are there per-connection limits we should be aware of? For example browsers opening many websockets for streaming.
08:06 - Diego Ramos: Websocket concurrencies are supported but we recommend aggregating streams with a gateway layer. For 300 concurrent users, websockets are fine but monitor file descriptors and NAT timeouts on your LB.
08:17 - Priya Singh: From a compliance spot, what's the default encryption-at-rest and key management for Hosted?
08:23 - Arjun Patel: Hosted encrypts at rest using provider-managed keys by default; for enterprise we support customer-managed KMS keys and optional HSM integrations. We can provide whitepapers and SOC artifacts.
08:35 - Lena Park: Good.
08:37 - Jordan Li: Any rough pricing delta between Hosted reserved capacity and Dedicated? We need to model economics.
08:44 - Maya Chen: Reserved Hosted gives a better start-for-free onboarding and lower up-front. Dedicated is priced as reserved GPU capacity — higher base cost but predictable latency and isolation. We'll send a custom TCO spreadsheet with model, expected tokens/sec, and burst factoring.
08:58 - Tomás Rivera: Will the pilot run on Hosted or Dedicated?
09:02 - Maya Chen: We usually pilot on Hosted (dedicated trial pool) to validate latency and then optionally migrate to Dedicated. You mentioned wanting to see Hosted numbers first so let's do Hosted pilot with reserved trial capacity.
09:12 - Priya Singh: We need to confirm that customer data is isolated during the Hosted pilot — at minimum end-to-end encryption and separate tenant keys.
09:19 - Diego Ramos: For pilot mode we can enable per-tenant encryption keys and isolate logs; we'll note the exact configurations.
09:27 - Jordan Li: On instrumentation, can we get per-request traces into our existing tracing stack (Jaeger/Tempo)?
09:33 - Arjun Patel: Yes, we'll integrate tracing hooks and provide a tracing sink or export. For Private, you control telemetry; for Hosted we can forward to your collector under an enterprise arrangement.
09:45 - Lena Park: Great. A few other quick technicalities: cold-start behavior for long tails, how we measure p99, and surge protection for token storms.
09:55 - Diego Ramos: For token storms our autoscaler supports burst capacity and automatic fallback policies. We'll include recommended autoscale windows and policies. For p99 and cold starts we'll run simulated evictions during the pilot to measure tail impact.
10:09 - Tomás Rivera: Any special notes about model compilation and kernel choices across CPU/GPU? We have an on-prem arm cluster we sometimes use for inference.
10:17 - Diego Ramos: Our compilation layer picks kernels based on hardware and seq len; ARM is supported but throughput differs. We'll include arm vs x86 numbers. Compilation also affects cold-start times so we'll measure that in pilot.
10:30 - Maya Chen: Let's summarize next steps before we run out of time.
10:34 - Maya Chen: Action items — we'll share a benchmark plan, starter harness, and pricing TCO. NorthForge will send the compliance checklist and a representative prompt set. We'll aim to kick the Hosted pilot next week if the paperwork is in place.
10:48 - Lena Park: Sounds good. Can we also get a written note on fallback policies and what data leaves our VPC during fallback?
10:55 - Arjun Patel: We'll produce a short security runbook that outlines exactly what payloads or logs move during a fallback and what is encrypted with CMK.
11:03 - Priya Singh: Also confirm the signed release process for Private images.
11:07 - Arjun Patel: Yes — we'll include image signing and the PKI flow in the runbook.
11:12 - Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the benchmark plan and propose dates for the pilot.
11:17 - Jordan Li: Thanks all, bye.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hear on acronyms (KV vs K-V), some names slightly off in auto-caption, filler words preserved.
questions: Can Redwood guarantee p95 <= 200ms for first token on short streaming flows under 300 concurrent users?
What is the expected tokens/sec per GPU for NorthForge prompt distribution across candidate models?
What audit and KMS options are available for Hosted pilot to satisfy SecOps?
